skyline.text: Amit Varma on why fretting about low-value tourists isn’t snobbery
How high-value tourists kept moving on, and why cricket is next
Freedom first, market failure next, and only then the state

footnote.text: It will take hundred years to become Switzerland.

brief.head: Tourists who fly
brief.text: Kangra’s runway is about 1,300 metres, Ajay Shah thinks, and Kullu’s about 1,100: too short for big aircraft. High-value tourists fly, so Himachal needs longer runways. {058-C10}

brief.head: When hardware sells
brief.text: Malini Goyal says Bangalore’s software is 5G but its hardware 2G. In Bir, Amit Varma said, the software is the hardware, and it must be made 5G. {058-J11}

brief.head: What’s in a name?
brief.text: By a lake in Udaipur, a year before launch, Amit Varma recalled, the hosts came up with two names: *Watching the Wheels* and *Everything is Everything*. {058-J10}

brief.head: Knobs for regions
brief.text: Steven Pinker’s line that nature gives us knobs and nurture turns them applies to regions too, Amit Varma suggested: each place has different knobs, so policy must fit. {058-J07}

brief.head: A reserve for two
brief.text: Ideally, Ajay Shah said, India and Nepal would run the Kangchenjunga reserve together. Sikkim’s part covers 2,000 of the state’s roughly 7,000 square kilometres, and Nepal holds another 2,000. {#sikkim}

thought.text: There is only one Himalayas in the entire planet Earth.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, making the case that the hills should build on what no one else has

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on tourism in the Himalayas
lead.head: Selling the view without losing it
body: The last of ten episodes recorded in a week at Bir, in Himachal Pradesh, grew out of a meeting with a viewer. Shubham Dhiman drove three hours from his village near Hamirpur to meet Amit Varma and Ajay Shah, and told them what he wanted.
“I don’t want to go and work in a city, I want to do something for Himachal,” Varma recalled him saying. {058-S01}
In Dhiman’s conversation with Shah, the question came up that this episode takes on: how can places like this develop without destroying what is already there?
Shah set the terms at once. The goal is sustained economic growth for the people of the Himalayan states, not scenery for outsiders.

“Sometimes there is an outsider’s condescending view that we want you to live at low levels of income because we would like your places to be nice for us,” he said. “And I’m not there at all.” {058-C01}
## Only one Himalayas

The plains recipe of factories, highways and modern farming would not work, Shah argued. The hill states are landlocked, far from the container ships, and mountain infrastructure is so costly that they would always do it worse than the plains.

Better to build on what no one else has. Switzerland and Colorado sell their beautiful locales, and their people have stayed prosperous for generations. “The glory of the Himalayan states is the Himalayas,” he said. {058-C03}
Udaipur had shown the way, he said, when Rajasthan gave its lakes first claim on scarce water, ahead of farming.
The people are not the obstacle once feared. Fertility is low across the hills and people are leaving them, Shah said, so the old worry about crowds clearing the forests is out of date.
## Where it goes wrong

Left alone, Shah said, every hotel and restaurant adds disco lights, loudspeakers and bonfires to pull in customers, and spoils the area around it. “They’ve just destroyed a circle with a radius of two hundred metres surrounding themselves.” {058-C06}
Tourism income is the number of tourists times what each spends. Chase the numbers and the big spenders go.

Dharamshala, near Bir, showed the result. Each step up the hill, from Dharamshala to McLeod Ganj to Dharamkot, enjoyed a good 20 or 30 years and then decayed into what Shah called “a stable equilibrium of poverty”.
Varma insisted that worrying about low-value tourists was not snobbery. In that equilibrium, he said, the locals earn less and the beauty is destroyed: “a lose-lose game”.
## Bir before Bangalore
Shah’s remedies were town planning and urban governance: lines on maps for streets and parks before building swallows the land, and a state that fines whoever lights a fire.

Small Bir, he argued, is a better bet than big Bangalore. Bangalore sells software, so its residents put up with a broken city. Bir sells itself. “So in Bangalore, people are much more casual about littering because their business is software.” {058-C09}
Parks, too, could earn far more, as America’s Yellowstone does.
None of it is quick, Shah warned. But the dream, he said, should be that Bir can become the Switzerland of India.

second.label: Rajasthan’s big bet
second.head: The lakes jump the queue
second.deck: Ajay Shah on how Rajasthan put tourism ahead of farming in Udaipur
body: Udaipur’s lakes used to depend on the monsoon, Ajay Shah said. In a good year the city was staggeringly beautiful. In others the water evaporated, and people would check with each other that “the lakes are nice” before going.

Then Vasundhara Raje, Rajiv Mehrishi and others changed Rajasthan’s rules for irrigation water: whatever the scarcity, Udaipur’s lakes would come first. Farmers lower in the queue lost out in the short term. {058-S02}

Shah called it a trivial calculation. Rajasthan is not a great place for agriculture, and Udaipur, “the Venice of the East”, now makes serious money from high-value tourism, with lakhs of people tied to its economy. {058-J12}

quote.text: Whatever be the scarcity of water, first, Udaipur lakes will get water.

third.head: Parks that pay their way
body: Indian national parks do two things well, Ajay Shah said: they stop poaching and they stop commercial development. What they have not done is earn. “We’ve not yet figured out how to contribute to the GDP.” {058-C11}
His headline was Yellowstone, in the United States. It gets four million tourists a year, he said, each spending between $1,000 and $2,000: four to eight billion dollars of revenue. {#yellowstone}

His model for the Great Himalayan National Park: beautiful gateway villages like Bir on its edge, hundreds of kilometres of walking trails inside, campgrounds, and a little high-end lodging run by private operators bound by strict biodiversity clauses.
Protecting wildlife and becoming a Switzerland, Shah said, can go together. “These goals are not inconsistent.”

p2.title: A hundred-year plan
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s case for how Himalayan states can prosper on their beauty, with Amit Varma asking the hard questions

sections.label: The strategy
sections.head: Not a hill-top Haryana
sections.caption: the plains recipe and the Himalayas
body: Ajay Shah calls himself an economic growth fundamentalist. So he framed the question as the path to sustained growth for the people of the Himalayan states, from Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh to Nepal, Bhutan and the North East. His only loyalty, he said, is to their welfare and livelihoods. {058-C01}
Amit Varma asked whether regions, like people, come with knobs of different sizes. Shah’s answer was the subsidiarity principle: the local political system should set its own priorities.

Haryana, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat have a standard recipe: build infrastructure, attract big factories, raise farm yields. It does not travel uphill. The Himalayan states are landlocked and will never have the coastline that opens up trade by container ship. Mountain airports, railways and highways cost so much that user charges would be very high.
## The asset nobody else has
Follow the plains recipe, Shah said, and “in a way you’re a bit doomed”, always doing it imperfectly, with a per capita GDP much worse than in the plains. {058-C02}
The alternative is to build on what nobody can copy. Switzerland and Colorado sell their beautiful locales, and tourism there is among the world’s most prosperous industries. {058-C03}
~ “Udaipur has its lakes and the Himalayan states have the Himalayas,” Shah said. The harder question was how to make that last.

quote.text: The airports, the highways, the railway lines in these states will always be 50% inferior to what is done in the plains.

sections.label: The people
sections.head: Fewer hands, empty homes
sections.caption: the hills’ demographic turn
body: Amit Varma turned from the place to its people. Two arguments, Ajay Shah said, could once have sunk a tourism strategy: too many workers for an industry that uses few, and so many people that forests would be cleared for farms and houses.

Those problems are largely behind us, he said. The total fertility rate in Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand is around 1.6 and 1.7, similar in Sikkim and Bhutan. Rapid population growth is a thing of the past. {058-C04}
Low birth rates and migration out of the hills mean projections of a gentle decline in the population and in the working-age population.
## Villages without people
In Uttarakhand there are more than 3,000 abandoned villages, Shah said, and he has hiked through them. {#villages} He has started to see the same in the deep Sahyadris.
Leaving is rational, he said. In the remote mountains a good life is hard to sustain, and people want to be nearer the cities.
~ The fear of humans clearing forests belonged to 1950 and 1960, Shah said. “But that’s not where we are today.”

quote.text: So the age of rapid population growth is over, in fact.

sections.label: The drift
sections.head: The 200-metre circle
sections.caption: the bonfire next door
body: What happens if nobody does anything? Amit Varma asked. Ajay Shah said the question applied the recipe of public economics: start from freedom and respect people’s creativity, find what goes wrong, and only then “start like John Maynard Keynes and wonder” whether the state can add value. {058-C05}

The story he told begins with one beautiful village, barely discovered. Word spreads like wildfire: first come the Instagrammers, then the YouTubers. {#instagram} Every local, in rational self-interest, wants to make money from it. Shacks and houses go up; then come traffic jams, disco lights and loudspeakers playing all night.
## A market failure hiding inside

Hiding inside this, Shah said, is a market failure: the negative externality. A pizza place that installs glitzy disco lights and five thousand watts of amplification thinks it is attracting tourists. In fact it has made a 200-metre zone around itself where nobody wants to go. {058-C06}
Let N be the number of tourists and P what each spends per day. A region’s tourism income is N times P. Maximise N, he said, and P falls: the high-value tourists stop coming.
~ Shah’s picture of an unmanaged Bir: five restaurants competing with “five thousand watts and ten thousand watts” and lights “blinking so that the aliens can see us from Alpha Centauri”. {058-J03}

quote.text: Start at the baseline, freedom is normal, people will do whatever they want.

sections.label: The trap
sections.head: Boom, bust, repeat
sections.caption: the low-income trap
body: Amit Varma said Ajay Shah’s forecast for Bir was not theory but practice: it had already happened, in the neighbourhood, in Dharamshala.

Shah described the pattern. A place gets twenty or thirty good years. Then it falls into a stable equilibrium of poverty, held there by low-value tourists, who do not need high human capital to serve them and who damage the place further. {058-C07}

Building human capital, he said, is a hundred-year journey. Sustainability means an arc of income that keeps rising over that span, as in Switzerland, Colorado and Japan, where people have gone back for generations.
## Not snobbery

Varma anticipated a charge. Talk of low-value tourists, he said, “sounds really snobbish”. But neither his view nor the visitors’ was the point. What mattered was how the local people and the local economy were doing.
A low-level equilibrium, he said, “almost seems like a lose-lose game”: locals make less money than they otherwise would, and everything beautiful about the place is gradually destroyed. {#loselose}
~ There are no quick fixes, Shah said, and no silver bullets. “It will take hundred years to become Switzerland.” But if things are done right, he said, the possibility is there. {#hundred}

quote.text: You get brief growth, it goes away. You get brief growth, it goes away.

sections.label: The toolkit
sections.head: Draw the streets first
sections.caption: lines on maps for Bir
body: What can be done? Ajay Shah’s answer came in two parts: town planning and urban governance, then parks. Much of what is known about cities, he said, carries straight over to the hills.

Bir has a landing zone for paragliders but no other parks. Following Bimal Patel, Shah would draw lines on maps now, setting aside 40 to 50 per cent of the land for streets and parks before unplanned building makes that impossible. {058-C08}
Across the road from the landing ground he imagined cafés and no vehicles, like the walking centre of a Swiss town. “So it becomes a walking zone where it can just be so beautiful.” {#walking}
## Who lit that fire?
Then public goods, such as clean air. Fires around Bir fill the air with smoke, and Shah would fine whoever lit one. {058-S05}
Amit Varma raised the obvious worry: high modernism, the top-down engineering mindset, demanded of an Indian state with low capability. {#modernism} Perhaps basic rule of law was the safer default.

~ Shah wanted rule of law too, but said urban market failures call for more. He rejects Indian-style planning that specifies every school and petrol pump. There is no running away from town planning, he said.

quote.text: You are stuck if you don’t have that forty, fifty percent of the land allocated to the streets and the parks.

sections.label: The proof
sections.head: Small town, better odds
sections.caption: why Bir beats Bangalore
body: Amit Varma agreed with all of it, and then worried about isomorphic mimicry: taking a vision of town planning and asking an Indian state to deliver it without the capability or the politics to do so. {#mimicry} Were there examples closer to home?
Ajay Shah named community successes he knew of in Meghalaya, Bhutan and Nepal, where people understood the downhill slide and came together.

But knowledge comes first, he said. Anyone trying to act on this should reach past normal Indian town planning to experts at the frontier, such as Bimal Patel, and draw on urban-governance hands such as Pritika Hingorani.

Bir is also a smaller problem. “You must learn to walk before you can run,” he said, a chapter title from *In Service of the Republic*, which he wrote with Vijay Kelkar. Reformers should learn in small towns first. {058-J13}
## Selling the place itself

And the incentives line up. Bangalore sells software, so residents grumble but put up with a broken city, while a predatory state extracts money from the software makers. Bir sells the place itself. {058-C09}
~ Udaipur shows the effect, Shah said. Its police treat a woman’s safety on the streets at 2 AM as make or break, because one bad event can cost the town millions of dollars. {#twoam}

quote.text: Whereas in Bir, what you’re selling is a beautiful village, is a beautiful town.

side.boxText: At a viewers’ meetup in Bir, Shubham Dhiman, who had driven three hours from a village near Hamirpur and done Takshashila’s public policy course, talked policy with Ajay Shah. Amit Varma’s first thought, he admitted, was “episode”. {058-J02}

contQuote.text: So this is how the Great Himalayan National Park can simultaneously serve the requirements of wildlife protection and biodiversity protection, but also cater to the goals of becoming a Switzerland and having a high per capita GDP.

p3.title: Tales from the hills
p3.deck: Four tales from the Himalayas and the Sahyadris, and what each one teaches

stories.start: So for me personally The journey of Dharamsala was an aha moment
stories.end: and upper Dharam court is rapidly going to get destroyed
stories.caption: Dharamshala’s slide uphill
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the hill town that taught him the problem
stories.head: Going downhill, moving uphill
body: For Ajay Shah, Dharamshala was an aha moment: the place where he understood how a hill town goes bad, and how the damage climbs uphill. Amit Varma had asked about it because it is literally in Bir’s neighbourhood.
The story begins with the Dalai Lama in 1959. The airport came, Shah thinks, in 1960 or so, and Dharamshala was great. {#dalai}

There was no Instagram then and there were no YouTubers, so the memo took time to get out. Fame spread quietly, by word of mouth and through the *Lonely Planet*, and more and more people started coming.
By the eighties, he said, Dharamshala was overcrowded. “It became a bad Indian city,” with all the problems of urban governance, and the high-value tourists moved up to McLeod Ganj.

McLeod Ganj worked for about twenty years before it, too, started going bad. The high-value tourists moved to Lower Dharamkot. When the bad things started happening there, they moved on to Upper Dharamkot.

Then came what Shah called “a very bad event”: Dharamshala’s rise as a cricket stadium. “And cricket unfortunately goes with very low value tourists,” he said. His prediction is that Upper Dharamkot will rapidly be destroyed. {058-S04}

~ Each place, he said, had its period of high value, rising property prices and human capital being built. Then the negative externalities kicked in, and it sank back into low-value tourism and a stable equilibrium of poverty.
stories.why: Without urban governance, decline comes as a staircase: a 20- or 30-year bloom, ruin by negative externalities, then the high-value visitors move further uphill. Each step leaves a town locked in low-value tourism.
stories.postscript: When Shah later blamed “the cricket people” again, Varma apologised: “we love cricket. All cricket people are not the same, we contain multitudes.” {058-J04}

stories.start: I want to point to a remarkable phenomenon that some people
stories.end: There were just no other people. Everybody had left. So this is deep sayadris.
stories.caption: the abandoned villages
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s hikes through India’s abandoned villages
stories.head: Two hundred houses, three families
body: On the way up to Panchachuli, Ajay Shah stayed in a village of about 200 houses where three families still lived. Each hiker was offered an entire house for the night. {058-S03}
On the Pindari Glacier trek he heard men talk of a pregnant woman whom four men had to carry on a stretcher for 20 kilometres to reach the nearest healthcare facility. {#stretcher}
Uttarakhand has more than 3,000 such villages, he said. In the remote mountains a good life is hard to sustain, and moving to the city is rational.

~ Now he sees it in the deep Sahyadris too. On a nine-day trek in January, the one on which he broke his ankle on the fifth day, he reached a village on day three with about twenty houses, one old man and one old woman. {#sahyadri}

quote.text: And there were three families living there. Meaning there were about 197 empty houses.

stories.start: Yesterday when we were up at Billing, standing at 2500 meters
stories.end: put a fine of ten thousand rupees on the person who lit the fire
stories.caption: the haze over Bir
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a view lost in smoke, and how to clear it
stories.head: Where there’s smoke, send a drone
body: The day before recording, the crew stood at Billing, 2,500 metres up, and looked down at Bir, 800 metres below. What they saw was a haze of solid particulate matter.
There were fires, Ajay Shah said, some perhaps lit by tourists with bonfires, “really the bad kinds of tourists”. From the landing ground below, you can barely see Billing.
Everybody’s view is damaged, he said, and the beauty of the whole place with it: a negative externality that no individual can fix. {058-S05} “Only the state can fix air quality in North India.”
~ His fix: put drones in the air to see every fire with thermal cameras, and send a policeman to fine whoever lit it ten thousand rupees. {#fine}
stories.why: Clean air and a clear view are public goods. A bonfire pleases one hotel’s guests and harms everyone, which is where even a freedom-first thinker says the state must act. {058-C05}

stories.start: there is a great man named Harish Kaparia. Uh he is a mountaineer
stories.end: So thank you, Harish Kapadya, you changed my life.
stories.caption: Harish Kapadia’s book
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the book that made him a hiker
stories.head: A book fair, then the Sahyadris
body: At about eleven, Ajay Shah walked into a book fair in Bombay and stumbled on *Trek the Sahyadris* by Harish Kapadia, a mountaineer and an enthusiast of the great outdoors in India. {#bookfair}
He bought it and read it a hundred times. Then, on his own, with no help and no knowledge, he and a bunch of other kids from Bandra East started hiking in the Sahyadris.
It was a turning point in his life, he said. “So thank you, Harish Kapadia, you changed my life.” {058-S06}
~ Kapadia has a new book from 2023, *Autumn Passage to the Himalaya*, which Shah called one of the lovely books for anyone who takes an interest in the Himalayas. {058-R04}
stories.why: One book, found by chance at the right age, can shape a whole life. Amit Varma suggested Shah could now be that spark for young people, and urged viewers to watch the hiking episode.

quiz.q: What did Rajasthan change so that Udaipur’s lakes would no longer depend on a good monsoon?
quiz.a: The irrigation rules: Udaipur’s lakes get water first, whatever the scarcity, ahead of farming.

quiz.q: Why, according to Ajay Shah, should Himachal Pradesh want longer airport runways?
quiz.a: High-value tourists fly; Kangra’s and Kullu’s short runways cannot take big aircraft.

quiz.q: Why does Ajay Shah fear for Upper Dharamkot now that Dharamshala hosts cricket?
quiz.a: Cricket brings very low-value tourists, and he predicts Upper Dharamkot will soon be destroyed.

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s formula for tourism income, what are N and P, and what goes wrong?
quiz.a: Tourist numbers and daily spend; chasing more tourists drives down what each one spends.

quiz.q: How would Ajay Shah stop the fires that fill Bir’s air with smoke?
quiz.a: Drones with thermal cameras to spot fires, and a ten-thousand-rupee fine for whoever lit them.

quiz.q: Which book, found at a Bombay book fair at about eleven, made Ajay Shah a hiker?
quiz.a: Harish Kapadia’s *Trek the Sahyadris*, which he read a hundred times.
